newsitem.title: USA: Some U.S. Gulf War vets said to have brain damage.
newsitem.headline: Some U.S. Gulf War vets said to have brain damage.

text.p: Some U.S. Gulf War veterans suffer from a form of brain damage found in victims of toxic poisoning, a group of U.S. doctors said in a study released Friday.

Researchers at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Centre said they performed neuropsychological tests on 46 Gulf War veterans from a U.S. Navy reserve unit, of whom 20 were healthy and 26 suffered from "Gulf War syndromes" such as memory and sleep problems, fatigue, confusion, imbalance and sore joints and muscles.
The ill veterans performed worse on 59 of 71 brain-related tests.

"Statistically, that is amazing," Dr. Jim Hom, who conducted the tests, told Reuters. "There is something wrong with these ill veterans that is clearly brain-related ... and it is very consistent with neurotoxic poisoning."
Tens of thousands of Gulf War veterans claim they were poisoned by a cocktail of chemicals given to them during the 1991 war to force Iraqi troops out of Kuwait.
They allegedly included anti-nerve gas pills, insect repellent and flea collars which were provided to U.S. troops as well as exposure to chemical nerve agents in battle.
Government officials have suggested that many of the problems faced by veterans were related to stress but Hom said his tests showed the damage suffered had nothing to do with stress.
"These are brain-related deficits that cannot be accounted for by psychological problems," he said, adding that the ill veterans showed a "global" pattern of damage affecting the entire brain.
He said the damage affected the ill veterans' memory, intelligence, attention span, use of language, hand-eye coordination and other brain functions.
The test results were very similar to those reported in a 1988 study of workers damaged by organophosphate poisons at work, the researchers said.

Hom conceded that the study sample was small but said it demonstrated the need for closer examination of the issue. "We need to go further in this direction and stop using stress as an excuse," he said.
